title: Table songs
tomorrow: the Torah never mentions phones. so why do some put them away?

segments.voice: Yesterday, one question from the portion, carried to dinner: Torah at the table. Tonight the same table gets louder.

Friday night, Noa's kitchen. The soup bowls are empty, the challah is down to crumbs, and nobody gets up. Saba David taps the table twice with a spoon and starts to hum. No words at first, just yai-dai-dai, low and slow. On the second round, Owen's grandfather finds a harmony underneath it. Noa, who swore she couldn't sing, drums on the table. By the third round the whole table is going, and nobody announced a song or handed out lyrics. So what just happened here, and why is it so much older than anyone at this table?
screen: `THE BOWLS ARE EMPTY. NOBODY GETS UP.` → `A SPOON TAPS TWICE.` → `YAI-DAI-DAI.` → `WHY IS THIS SO OLD?`

segments.voice: What happened is zemirot: table songs, sung at Shabbat meals, between courses or before the blessing after eating. The word means songs, and a Psalm uses it: "Thy statutes have been my songs." The idea runs back to the Temple. The Mishnah lists a psalm the Levites sang there for each day of the week, and for Shabbat it was the one titled "A Psalm, a Song. For the sabbath day." Then the Temple was gone, and the Talmud says something startling: once the altar atoned for Israel; now a person's table does. If the table stands in for the altar, it gets the altar's music too. So the songs moved from the Temple courts to the kitchen. Over the centuries poets kept writing new ones, in Hebrew and Aramaic. One table favorite, Yah Ribon, by the poet Israel Najara, opens in Aramaic: God, master of the world and of all worlds. Some tables sing a niggun instead, a tune with no words at all, which is exactly what Saba was doing. That's the part to tell a friend tonight: you don't need to know the words to join. A hum counts. Zemirot aren't a test you can fail; they're closer to a family singing at a birthday, except this birthday comes every week. The point isn't a performance. It's a table that doesn't want the meal to end.
screen: `ZEMIROT: TABLE SONGS.` · `A PSALM FOR THE SABBATH DAY.` · `THE TABLE IN PLACE OF THE ALTAR.` · `A NIGGUN: NO WORDS NEEDED.` · then, large: `SING AT THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Pick one tune you can carry: a Shabbat song you know, a melody from your own family, or just yai-dai-dai. Hum it once softly, then once a little louder, tapping the beat on a table or your knee. If no tune comes, hum one low note on each out-breath and let that be your song.
Zemirot: table songs. Sung at Shabbat meals, from the Temple's psalm to a wordless hum over the crumbs.
Pocket this one: sing at the table, even if a hum is all you've got. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: At Shabbat dinner and lunch, families sing zemirot between courses or before the blessing after the meal, from small songbooks or by heart; some tables sing wordless tunes, called niggunim.
